notes: Brief procedural judgment refusing a section 33 certificate; jurisdictional point on leave to appeal is clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Moulden: no House of Lords appeal from refusal of leave to appeal
key_facts: Leslie Moulden sought a renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction, sentence and a confiscation order, all refused on 27 October 2004.
He then sought a certificate that a point of law of general public importance was involved and leave to appeal to the House of Lords under section 33(2).
The whole Court of Appeal considered the application but refused a certificate because it would serve no useful purpose.
The court held that the House of Lords had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from a decision refusing leave to appeal rather than deciding an appeal under Part 1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal for a section 33 certificate and leave to appeal to the House of Lords after refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Certificate refused; no leave to appeal to the House of Lords because the October 2004 decision was not a decision on an appeal.
enrichment.ratio: An application for leave to appeal is not an appeal within section 33(1) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968; accordingly the House of Lords has no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from a refusal of leave, following R v Mealey and Sheridan.
legal_issues: Whether a refusal of leave to appeal is a decision on an appeal within section 33(1)
Whether a certificate of a point of law of general public importance should be granted
Whether an oral hearing was required on the certificate application
index_terms: point of law of general public importance
linked_authorities: R v Mealey and Sheridan [1975] Crim LR 154

notes: Asperger's contact appeal; Potter and Wall LJJ's expert/guardian guidance is detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Re C: Asperger's child contact and section 91(14) order set aside
key_facts: R, a 14-year-old boy with Asperger's Syndrome, firmly refused direct contact with his father after years of litigation.
HHJ Cliffe dismissed the father's further contact application and made a section 91(14) order barring applications until 1 August 2005.
The father sought NYAS appointment as guardian, expert evidence on autistic spectrum disorders and transfer to the High Court.
The judge found nothing had changed since July 2004 and that further orders would be counterproductive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal with appeal to follow against dismissal of contact application and a section 91(14) order in the York County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 91(14) order set aside, judge's dismissal set aside, R joined as party with NYAS appointed guardian and papers to be supplied within seven days.
enrichment.ratio: Where a devoted parent seeks contact with a child who rejects him for reasons explicable only by a psychiatric disorder, a judge should not cut off contact without expert guidance on autistic spectrum disorders; section 91(14) should not ordinarily be imposed at short notice on a litigant in person without exceptional justification.
legal_issues: Whether expert evidence on Asperger's Syndrome was required before refusing contact
Whether the section 91(14) order complied with Re P guidelines
Whether R should be separately represented and whether NYAS rather than CAFCASS should be guardian
Whether the case should be transferred to the High Court or heard by a different judge
index_terms: Re C prohibition on further applications
linked_authorities: Re P (Section 91(14) Guidelines) (Residence and Religious Heritage) [1999] 2 FLR 592
Re C (Prohibition on Further Applications) [2002] EWCA Civ 292

notes: Somalia asylum/human rights permission application; Robinson 'obvious point' test applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Mahamoud: no obvious Article 3 point on Somalia civil war risk
key_facts: Layla Esse Mahamoud, a Somali national, appealed removal directions after her asylum and human rights claims were refused.
She claimed harassment, violence and rape by members of a rival sub-clan over several years before fleeing Somalia.
The adjudicator disbelieved most of her account after 1998 and treated Articles 2 and 3 as raising the same factual issues as the asylum claim.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal and Court of Appeal refused permission, holding no obvious Convention point had been overlooked.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; detailed assessment of costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator or tribunal need consider only obvious points of Convention law with a strong prospect of success if not raised by the appellant; where personal persecution claims were disbelieved, a general reference to civil war risk in Somalia did not require separate Article 3 analysis, applying ex parte Robinson.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in failing to assess risk from Somalia's civil war under Articles 2 and 3
Whether an obvious human rights point arose despite disbelief of the appellant's personal account
Whether the IAT erred in refusing leave to appeal
linked_authorities: R v Home Secretary, ex parte Robinson [1998] QB 929

notes: Landmark EU indirect discrimination appeal on income support absence rule; O'Flynn principles applied without statistics.

enrichment.short_title: Bobezes: indirect nationality discrimination in income support child absence rule

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr Bobezes, a Portuguese migrant worker, received income support including dependent child allowance for his stepdaughter Sonia.
The Secretary of State recovered £525 overpaid allowance because Sonia spent periods exceeding four weeks in Portugal with her grandmother.
Regulation 16(5) of the Income Support (General) Regulations 1987 disapplied household membership where a child was continuously absent from Great Britain for more than four weeks.
Bobezes argued the rule indirectly discriminated against migrant workers whose children were more likely to stay abroad with family.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a Social Security Commissioner's decision remitting indirect discrimination issues to the appeal tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal on Regulation choice not pursued; cross-appeal allowed so the tribunal must decide whether discrimination is justified under Regulation 1408/71 Article 3.
enrichment.ratio: A nationality-neutral provision is indirectly discriminatory if intrinsically liable to affect migrant workers more than national workers; statistical proof is not required where the risk arises from the normal separation of migrant workers' families, following O'Flynn, Pinna and Biehl.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 1408/71 or 1612/68 governed the claim
Whether Regulation 16(5) indirectly discriminated against migrant workers
Whether statistical evidence was required to establish indirect discrimination
Whether Perry v Chief Adjudication Officer barred the claim
linked_authorities: O'Flynn v Adjudication Officer (Case C-237/94) [1996] ECR I-2617
Pinna v Caisse d'Allocations Familiales de la Savoie (Case 41/84) [1986] ECR 1

notes: Closure order adjournment case stated; Mitting J's section 54 analysis is of general magistrates' court importance.

enrichment.short_title: Metropolitan Police v Hooper: closure order adjournment powers under section 54
key_facts: Police issued a closure notice and applied for a closure order under section 2 of the 2003 Act in respect of premises linked to Class A drug use and nuisance.
Tenant Karen Hooper sought to oppose the application; magistrates adjourned on 7 and 15 July 2004 for fairness and because she had suffered a head injury.
The second adjournment exceeded 14 days after the initial application, contrary to section 2(6) but magistrates relied on inherent powers.
The application was later dismissed for want of prosecution on 12 August 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated on statutory construction and magistrates' adjournment powers in section 2 closure order proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Magistrates acted outside section 2(6) powers but had section 54 power to adjourn exceptionally; their exercise was flawed for failing to consider statutory purpose and section 2(7).
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(6) permits adjournment for up to 14 days after application to allow interested parties to show cause, but section 54 remains available in exceptional circumstances compatible with Convention rights and the Act's purpose of speedy closure of disorderly premises; magistrates have no general inherent adjournment power.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 proceedings are civil or criminal for Convention purposes
Whether magistrates could adjourn more than once or beyond 14 days under section 2(6)
Whether section 54 or inherent powers permitted further adjournment
What factors magistrates must consider when exercising section 54

R (Mathialagan) v London Borough of Southwark [2004] EWCA Civ 1689
R v Dudley Magistrates' Court ex parte Hollis [1999] 1 WLR 1999

notes: Jury internet research appeal; Judge LJ's open justice rationale following Mirza is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Karakaya: convictions quashed after juror downloaded rape material from internet

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Adem Karakaya was convicted of indecent assault and rape of his 17-year-old daughter at Canterbury Crown Court in November 2003.
After overnight adjournment of jury deliberations, a juror downloaded internet material on rape and the criminal justice system into the jury room.
The documents included tendentious and inaccurate material critical of conviction rates and judges' summings up.
The jury bailiff discovered the material after verdicts; no enquiry was made of jurors but the Court of Appeal examined it under Mirza.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on the ground that extraneous material introduced after retirement rendered the verdict unsafe.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on 2 February; convictions quashed and a new trial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A juror must not conduct private research or introduce extraneous material after retirement; such conduct contravenes open justice and the parties' fair opportunity to address all material considered by the jury, following Owen, Wilson, Davis and Mirza.
legal_issues: Whether internet material downloaded by a juror after retirement was admissible extraneous evidence
Whether the convictions were safe despite majority verdicts
Whether handwritten jury notes could be examined on appeal
What directions should warn juries against internet research
linked_authorities: R v Mirza; R v Connor and Rollock [2004] 1 AC 1118
Owen [1952] 36 CAR 16
Davis [1976] 62 CAR 194

notes: Landmark Hunting Act/Parliament Act validity appeal; full constitutional analysis with appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Jackson v Attorney General: validity of Parliament Act 1949 and Hunting Act 2004
key_facts: Countryside Alliance members challenged the validity of the Hunting Act 2004, enacted under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949.
The 1949 Act reduced the Lords' delaying period under the 1911 Act from two years to one year and was itself passed without Lords consent.
Claimants argued the Commons could not use the 1911 procedure to amend the conditions on which that power was granted.
The Administrative Court dismissed the claim; urgent appeal was heard before the Hunting Act's commencement date of 19 February 2005.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Administrative Court on whether the 1949 Act and Hunting Act were valid Acts of Parliament.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the 1949 Act was a lawful modification of the 1911 Act and the Hunting Act was valid, but greater constitutional changes could fall outside the 1911 Act's scope.
enrichment.ratio: Legislation passed under the Parliament Act 1911 is subordinate to that enabling Act; a modest reduction of the delaying period from two years to one was within the 1911 Act's scope, but use of the procedure to abolish the Lords or extend Parliament's life beyond five years would not be.
legal_issues: Whether courts could adjudicate on the validity of an Act receiving Royal Assent
Whether the 1949 Act was primary or delegated legislation
Whether the 1911 Act authorised amendment of its own procedural conditions without Lords consent
What limits apply to constitutional change via the Parliament Acts
linked_authorities: Edinburgh and Dalkeith Railway Co v Wauchope (1842) 8 Cl & F 710
Bribery Commissioner v Ranasinghe [1965] AC 172
McCawley v The King [1920] AC 691

notes: Disabled adult housing JR; Mitting J's section 21 adapted accommodation analysis extends Help the Aged principles.

enrichment.short_title: Hughes v Liverpool: section 21 duty for specially adapted accommodation

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970

key_facts: Kenny Hughes, born 6 April 1985, has severe cerebral palsy, learning difficulties, epilepsy and declining mobility and lives with his mother in unsuitable upstairs accommodation.
Liverpool accepted from April 2003 that the property was unsuitable but failed to provide adapted ground-floor housing until at least August 2005.
The council also failed to provide promised weekend respite care despite identifying eligible welfare needs in a January 2004 assessment.
Mrs Hughes brought judicial review for breach of sections 21 and 29 duties and an Article 8 damages claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Liverpool City Council's failure to provide suitable accommodation and welfare services for a severely disabled adult.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that Liverpool was in breach of section 21; orders for weekend respite within 28 days and reassessment within 28 days; Article 8 damages claim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 21 of the 1948 Act applies where a disabled person needs specially adapted accommodation beyond ordinary Part VII priority need housing; section 21(8) does not exclude that duty where Part VII provides only generic homelessness accommodation.
legal_issues: Whether section 21 or Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 governed the accommodation claim
Whether Liverpool breached its section 21 duty since the claimant turned 18
Whether eligible welfare needs including respite care had been met under section 29 guidance
Whether Article 8 required damages for breach of statutory duties

notes: School DDA respondent and justification appeal; Keene LJ's employment powers analysis follows Green.

enrichment.short_title: Murphy v Slough: governing body as DDA employer for paid maternity leave refusal

statutes_considered.title: Education (Modification of Enactments Relating to Employment) Order 1999

key_facts: Mrs Murphy, a teacher at Langleywood School with a congenital heart disorder, sought paid leave to bond with a child born through a US surrogate.
The governing body granted only unpaid leave because the school budget was in deficit after special measures and the LEA refused contingency funding.
Her contract was with Slough LEA but staffing powers at the delegated-budget school rested with the governing body under Schedule 16.
The employment tribunal held the governing body alone was the correct respondent and that refusal of paid leave was justified.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on the correct DDA respondent and justification of refusing paid leave.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; governing body was the sole proper respondent when refusing paid leave in exercise of employment powers, and justification was established.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1999 Order a school governing body is the DDA employer only when exercising employment powers conferred by Schedule 16; the power to grant or refuse paid leave falls within paragraph 22 discipline and conduct regulation, so only the governing body is liable, following Green v Victoria Road Primary School.
legal_issues: Whether the LEA, governing body or both were proper respondents to DDA claims by a maintained school teacher
Whether refusal of paid leave was an exercise of employment powers
Whether justification under sections 5(3) and 5(4) was correctly applied
Whether section 6(4) factors were wrongly considered at the justification stage

notes: Auction contract and vendor-trustee summary judgment; Lawrence Collins J's trustee duty scope analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Englewood v Patel: auction buyer liability and vendor trustee duty on adjoining lots
key_facts: Englewood sold a Woolworths parade shop at auction to Mr Patel's bid of £1,320,000; Cornberry Ltd was later named as buyer and paid the deposit.
The October 1939 lease contained a lessor covenant restricting letting adjoining shops to fixed-price retailers competing with Woolworths.
Englewood sold other parade lots at the same auction without inserting protective covenants, creating a title defect valued at £800,000.
Buyers refused completion claiming breach of vendor's trustee duty and sought abatement; Englewood sought specific performance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment ordering specific performance against auction buyers who resisted on agency and vendor breach of duty grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Mr Patel remained personally liable under auction conditions and no arguable vendor trustee duty required covenant imposition on adjoining lot purchasers.
enrichment.ratio: Auction conditions imposing personal liability on a bidder bind an agent even where the auctioneer knows he acts as agent; a vendor's equitable trusteeship between contract and completion requires preservation of the property sold but does not extend to imposing covenants on purchasers of separate adjoining lots unless the contract so requires.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Patel escaped personal liability as agent or by estoppel when Cornberry Ltd was treated as buyer
Whether Englewood breached trustee duties by selling other lots without anti-competition covenants
Whether separate simultaneous auction lots should be treated as one transaction for trust purposes
Whether buyers were entitled to abatement for the title defect
linked_authorities: Lysaght v Edwards (1876) 2 Ch D 499
Rayner v Preston (1881) 18 Ch D 1
Abdulla v Shah [1959] AC 124
